# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the basics pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- running-the-suite: Running this repo's test suite — the one command that covers it, reading a run's output from a file instead of re-running it, iterating on the tests an edit touches, and staging a new test file before certifying a run. Use before any node --test.
- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, get the owner's approval of the plan itself — a line per step, the dependency graph, each link's automerge policy — before filing any of its issues, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, size the links (how many PRs, what each one's diff is predicted to touch and the automerge policy that prediction becomes) and write the chain to survive a policy park, a red CI or a PR closed unmerged, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, page numbers, or letterheads. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. claudinite-canary-repo The canon's live proof that it can deliver a file into a member's `.github/workflows/`. ## Why it exists `.github/workflows/` is the one directory the nightly update can never push to. The update commits with the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, GitHub refuses that token under that path, and the refusal rejects the **whole ref** — so a single workflow write does not fail one file, it fails the entire converge and everything riding it. #649 is that problem. The answer is the **withhold lane** in the pack update flow: every write bound for `.github/workflows/` is diverted to `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`, a path the Action token *can* push. It rides the maintenance PR as an ordinary added file — reviewable in the diff, recoverable if nothing else runs — and the update ends at `apply-stage` until a session holding an MCP credential moves it into place. That lane shipped with **one** exercised caller: the scheduler workflow's own convergence. A record's `materialize` goes through the same `write`, and had never run against a live member — the residual #649 was reopened for, and the last item left on #768. Proving it needs a record that materializes a workflow into a repo that really runs the update flow, and nothing in the corpus was one. This pack is that. ## What it ships | | | |---|---| | [`stubs/workflows/claudinite-workflow-probe.yml`](stubs/workflows/claudinite-workflow-probe.yml) | one inert workflow — `workflow_dispatch` only, no schedule, no push | | `seedOps` | seeds that file at **adoption**, written by the install flow and committed by the adopting session | | [`migrations/2026-08-14-workflow-probe-current/`](migrations/2026-08-14-workflow-probe-current/migration.mjs) | from pack version 2 on, re-vendors the same path through the withhold lane | The two routes are the point, and their order is the point. Seeding is the easy half — the adopting session holds a credential the Action token does not, so nothing is being tested there. The record is the hard half, and because the file is already present by then, it has to *update* a workflow rather than create one — the exact shape a fleet-wide workflow fix would take. ## Who carries it `seededByDefault: false`, `detect: null`, `marker: null`. `--init` never seeds it, the fleet's pack scan never suspects it, and a repo carries it only because someone declared it by hand. The intended holder is **the canary** and nothing else: a probe belongs on the repo that exists to be converged against candidate refs and is disposable by construction. ## Reading the result The workflow's one step echoes a **revision marker**. "The file exists" stops being an assertion once the file has existed since adoption, so a delivery is watched by bumping that line in the template here and checking the member's copy against it. Current marker: **revision 2**. A member whose copy reads `revision 2` was reached by the *record*, through the withhold lane — staged into `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`, carried in a maintenance PR, and moved into `.github/workflows/` by a session with a credential the Action token does not have. `revision 1` means the seed landed and the record has not run yet.

## Normalize requirements to canonical form at the door

When a requirement arrives expressed in someone's local context — a schedule in a local
timezone, a path from one repo's layout, a phrasing tied to one project's vocabulary — we
currently translate it to its canonical form **once, on the way in**, and record only the
result. A "nightly at 3:30 my time" request lands in the canon as a fixed UTC cron, stated in
UTC and nothing else. The reasoning: the person who asked can carry the original framing;
consumers shouldn't inherit it, and the canon shouldn't have to re-explain a conversion (or its
edge cases, like DST) forever. If the origin matters for revisiting the decision, it belongs in
the issue/PR that made the change, not in the shipped artifact.

## How to prove a change is consumer-safe

Canon CI is not evidence about consumers. The canon's own packs are always already migrated, so a
change that breaks every member passes it green — which is exactly what #555 did, on 2026-07-29,
while eleven consumer packs stopped validating and (because a pack that fails validation
contributes no rules) their checks stopped running with no other symptom.

So there is a procedure, in three layers, cheapest first.

**1. The fixture rehearsal — automatic, every PR.** `vendoring/rehearsal/` builds four fixture
consumers, one per shape the fleet has, and runs the REAL converge against your working tree:
`apply-vendor-set` → `converge-wiring` → `engine/migrations/apply`, then `engine/selftest.mjs` and
`check_the_world`. It runs in **two modes**, and the second is the half people forget:

| mode | stamp | answers |
|---|---|---|
| `fresh` | now | does the ordinary nightly path still work? |
| `stale` | pinned in the past | **does it work WITH a migration?** — note selection only fires against an old stamp, so a record that is missing, misdated, or not idempotent shows up here and nowhere else |

Adding a shape is the cheap way to cover a case the fixtures don't: a new entry in
`fixtures.mjs` is a few lines, and it is one of the two things that discharge the
`consumer-safe-change` check.

**2. The `consumer-safe-change` check — automatic, work scope.** A change touching a contract
consumers hold a copy of (the manifest vocabulary, a blocking rule's severity, the scheduler stub)
must ship **either** a migration record **or** a rehearsal fixture. They answer different
questions — *members are moved across* versus *members are unharmed* — and both are legitimate.
A genuinely additive change needs only the fixture; anything that renames or requires something
needs the record, because only a record moves a member that is already out there.

**3. The live canary — the required final step of any core change.** A fixture only tests what
someone remembered to model. `.github/workflows/canary-rehearsal.yml` converges a real disposable
repo against a canon ref and asks whether it still works: manually via `workflow_dispatch`, and
automatically on merge to `main`. Post-merge is still worth having — knowing within minutes beats
finding out from the fleet two days later, which is how long #585 went unnoticed.

Run it by hand before merging anything structural:
`gh workflow run canary-rehearsal.yml -f ref=<your-branch>`. The worker's rehearsal mode converges,
reports, and **restores** — no commit, no branch, no stamp. That last one matters: stamping a branch
head leaves the member `ref-not-on-trunk`, which the #328 anti-rewind guard then refuses to converge
over, so a careless rehearsal wedges the repo it was rehearsing on. That is not hypothetical; it
happened by hand to all thirteen members at once on 2026-07-30.

**What none of this covers.** A change whose damage is invisible to both the self-test and the
conformance sweep — a behaviour change inside a task, say — is still on you to reason about. The
layers narrow the class; they do not close it.

content.content:
# The LIVE CANARY (#593 phase 3) — the required final step of any core change.
#
# The fixture rehearsal (vendoring/rehearsal/) is the fast gate: hermetic,
# seconds, on every PR. It has one honest weakness — a fixture only tests what
# someone remembered to model. This is the other half: a REAL repo, really
# adopting Claudinite, really running its own scheduler, converged against this
# canon ref and asked whether it still works.
#
# WHY IT IS A SEPARATE WORKFLOW. It takes minutes, needs a cross-repo token, and
# mutates another repository's working tree. A gate with those properties cannot
# run on every push without becoming something people route around. So: manual
# dispatch, plus automatic on merge to main — the post-merge smoke test, which
# the owner's own framing settles as "still much much better than not knowing".
#
# WHERE THE CANARY IS NAMED. In `.claudinite-settings.json`, on the `local/claudinite`
# pack entry's `config.canaryRepo` — the same tracked pack-entry config mechanism
# the claudinite-fleet-sheepdog pack uses for its fleet scope. NOT a GitHub repository variable: the
# binding between this canon and its canary is a fact about the project, and a
# repository variable is invisible in the tree, absent from every diff, and cannot
# be reviewed alongside the workflow that acts on it. A reader of this repo should
# be able to see which repo CI is about to rewrite.
#
# WHY A DEDICATED REPO, NOT A REAL PROJECT. A rehearsal rewrites the mount and
# can leave a failed converge behind. Pointing that at EdFringeNow means a bad
# canon commit leaves a real project dirty at the exact moment attention is
# elsewhere. The canary is disposable by construction; that is its whole value.
#
# WHAT PROTECTS THE CANARY ITSELF: the worker's rehearsal mode
# (CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF) converges, reports, and then RESTORES the working tree —
# no commit, no branch, no PR, and above all no stamp. Stamping a branch head
# would leave the canary `ref-not-on-trunk`, which vendoring's #328 anti-rewind
# guard then refuses to converge over: a rehearsal that wedges its own canary.
name: Canary rehearsal

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      ref:
        description: "Canon ref to rehearse (blank = this workflow's own ref)"
        required: false
        type: string
  push:
    branches: [main]
    # Only the surfaces a consumer actually vendors. A README or a doc change
    # cannot break a member, and spending minutes proving that teaches everyone
    # to ignore the result.
    paths:
      - 'engine/**'
      - 'packs/**'
      - 'vendoring/**'

permissions:
  contents: read

# The rehearse step pipes into tee, and GitHub's implicit `bash -e` has no
# pipefail — a worker exiting non-zero into a successful tee would show green.
defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

concurrency:
  # One canary at a time: two rehearsals converging the same repo would race on
  # its working tree and report each other's damage.
  group: canary-rehearsal
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  rehearse:
    name: Rehearse against the canary repo
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - name: Check out the canon (for the declaration)
        uses: actions/checkout@v5

      - name: Resolve the canary repo from the declaration
        id: cfg
        run: |
          CANARY=$(node -e '
            const c = require("./.claudinite-settings.json");
            const e = (c.packs || []).find((p) => p && p.id === "local/claudinite");
            process.stdout.write(e?.config?.canaryRepo ?? "");
          ')
          if [ -z "$CANARY" ]; then
            echo "::warning::No canary declared — skipping the live canary."
            echo "Add config.canaryRepo to the local/claudinite pack entry in"
            echo ".claudinite-settings.json, naming a disposable repo that has adopted"
            echo "Claudinite. Until then the fixture rehearsal is the only consumer gate."
            echo "skip=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "Canary: $CANARY (from .claudinite-settings.json)"
            echo "skip=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "repo=$CANARY" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          fi

      - name: Check out the canary
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.skip == 'false'
        uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          repository: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.repo }}
          token: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          path: canary

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.skip == 'false'
        with:
          node-version: '24'

      # WHICH WORKER RUNS, and why it changed (#768 Phase 5). This drove the CANARY'S
      # OWN vendored worker on the argument that it is the copy a member would run.
      # That argument breaks on the case the gate exists for: the worker is itself
      # vendored content, so a change TO the worker cannot be rehearsed by the copy
      # that predates it — the member's vendored copy is by definition one release
      # behind, and a release is exactly what this is qualifying. So the worker under
      # test is the one THIS REF SHIPS, run against the canary's real tree; it is the
      # code every member will run the moment this release reaches them.
      #
      # The old path is also what made this gate VACUOUS for weeks: the canary flipped
      # to the update mechanism, the baselining worker this step pointed at correctly
      # stood down, and the step passed in zero seconds having converged nothing.
      # Hence the marker check below — a rehearsal that does not say it converged is
      # not a pass, whatever its exit code.
      - name: Rehearse
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.skip == 'false'
        env:
          CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF: ${{ inputs.ref || github.ref_name }}
          CLAUDINITE_REPO_ROOT: ${{ github.workspace }}/canary
          CLAUDINITE_REPO: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.repo }}
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        working-directory: packs/claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update
        run: node worker.mjs | tee "$RUNNER_TEMP/rehearsal.log"

      # A green step is not evidence; the marker is. Without this, every way of
      # exiting 0 without converging — a stand-down, an early return, a worker whose
      # path moved again — reads exactly like a qualified release.
      - name: Assert the rehearsal actually converged
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.skip == 'false'
        run: |
          if ! grep -q 'claudinite-rehearsal: converged' "$RUNNER_TEMP/rehearsal.log"; then
            echo "::error::The rehearsal exited 0 without converging the canary — it printed no"
            echo "::error::'claudinite-rehearsal: converged' line. A pass here would qualify a"
            echo "::error::release nothing rehearsed. Check the worker path in this workflow."
            exit 1
          fi

      - name: What a failure means
        if: failure()
        run: |
          echo "::error::The canary repo could not be converged against this canon ref."
          echo "A real consumer, on its real mount, either failed the self-test or went"
          echo "red on its own conformance sweep. This is the failure mode the fixture"
          echo "rehearsal is designed to catch early and the fleet is designed never to"
          echo "see: do not merge (or, post-merge, revert) until the canary is green."

        if: failure()

days stale: a plain `git fetch origin main` (no --unshallow) brought the

missing history depth rather than a reflex for a stuck ref.

# The repo's test/CI flow. Today it holds one step: the Claudinite WORLD-SCOPE
# sweep (bootstrap.md Part 8) — a whole-repo invariant assertion, the same shape as
# a test suite, so a red sweep fails this flow exactly like a failing test would.
# The WORK scope is not here: it judges a session's own change and runs at that
# session's Stop hook.
#
# When this repo grows tests of its own, they go in as further steps of this job —
# not as a second workflow.
name: Checks

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          # The sweep's default scope compares against origin/main, so the
          # history it measures from has to be here.
          fetch-depth: 0

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'

      # The engine's always-vendored Node CLI, invoked as the standalone command.
      - name: Claudinite world sweep
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs

# Fetching from the web

- **Needing exact text** — a summarizing fetch tool is not a source; when the bytes matter, `curl`
  into the scratchpad and read from disk.
- **A `403`** — don't retry and don't try a sibling URL; attribute the search snippet to the
  publisher instead of asserting it, and mark it for re-verification.
- **A sandbox or proxy denial is a policy boundary, not an obstacle to route around** — no
  open-network runner, no ad-hoc CI workflow, no push-triggered probe to make the request from
  somewhere the policy does not apply. Answer from committed reference material or ask the owner,
  and say plainly that anything unverifiable is unverified.
- **An explicit egress block** (`EGRESS_BLOCKED`) is domain-wide, unlike a publisher's `403`:
  working down alternate sources for the same fact spends the same denial on each. Never file the
  gap as "re-verify next pass" — no later agent pass can cross a policy block either; mark it as
  needing a human or an unblocked environment.

content.text:
I traced both. Here's what the evidence says.

## 1. What broke

**PR [missingbulb/Claudinite#1754](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1754)** (`db9981f`, "Keep Claudinite's own bookkeeping inside `.claudinite/`") removed the pack-badge-row mechanism from `engine/converge-wiring.mjs` — including the exported constants `BADGE_ROW_START` / `BADGE_ROW_END` / `README`, and the `--badges` flag.

The three `ensure*` functions it also removed **were** given re-export shims (`converge-wiring.mjs:191-195`). The badge constants were not.

Shepherd's own local pack imports them:

```
.claudinite/local/packs/shepherd/worldRules/pack-badge-row.mjs:2
  import { BADGE_ROW_START, BADGE_ROW_END, README } from '.../shared/engine/converge-wiring.mjs';
```

Last night's converge delivered the new engine, the module failed to load, and `check_the_world` reported it as **blocking** under `config` → the converged tree failed its self-test → [PR #477](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/pull/477) is labelled `needs-human` and sits open. That part is working as designed: nothing merges on a non-green terminal, and there is no agentic lane behind it by construction.

Same change left a second, quieter break: **`packs/claudinite-lifecycle/RULES.md:23` still tells every session in every member to run `converge-wiring.mjs <owner/repo> --badges`** — a flag that no longer exists. That rule is live in my own loaded prose right now.

## 2. Why the canary didn't catch it — it structurally cannot

Both consumer gates are blind to this exact class.

- **The live canary** (`ClaudiniteCanary`): I cloned it and grepped its local pack. Not one of its four world rules imports anything out of `.claudinite/shared/` — `realism-artifacts.mjs:12` says so as a stated design property: *"Dependency-free: plain finding objects, no imports out of `.claudinite/shared/`."* So a rehearsal converges the canary green no matter what the engine's export surface does.
- **The fixture rehearsal** (`vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs`): zero fixture local-pack files import an engine module either. The only `shared/engine` string in the file is inside a prose snippet.
- **`consumer-safe-change`**: deliberately narrow to three surfaces — `pack-schema.mjs`, a rule's `severity`, and the two workflow stubs. An engine module's *exported symbols* are not among them, so #1754 merged with no migration record and no fixture, correctly per the check as written.

So the gap isn't that the canary failed. It's that **member local-pack code importing engine surfaces is a real, corpus-encouraged contract** (Shepherd's rule also imports `findings.mjs` and `pack-registry.mjs`) **that nothing treats as a contract.** The canon's own rule already names the shape one rung down — *"Renaming or deleting an `engine/` module a `packs/` file imports — leave a shim"* — but it stops at modules, and its stated audience is canon packs, not members' local packs.

## 3. Why the run needed approval

Verified: attempt 1 was created at `2026-09-06T08:42:17Z`, three seconds after the PR opened, and **never produced a job at all** — `list_workflow_jobs` with `filter: all` returns exactly one job, `run_attempt: 2`, started `2026-09-07T05:43:03Z` with `triggering_actor: missingbulb`. So it was held, not run-and-rerun. That matches what you saw.

What I could **not** verify is *why* GitHub held it. Repo-scoped `api.github.com` is 403'd from this session, the held attempt's own record is gone once attempt 2 superseded it, and no MCP tool reads repository Actions settings. Two things argue against the obvious "it's a bot PR" answer: the 09-03 and 09-05 update PRs, same `github-actions[bot]` actor, started instantly; and the usage-fold PR **two minutes later** on 09-06 ([run 34022708608](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/actions/runs/34022708608)) also started instantly. Whatever it was, it was specific to that run, not a policy flip.

The cheapest primary source is one you have and I don't: the held run's own banner in the UI names the reason ("This workflow requires approval from a maintainer" vs. a first-time-contributor wording). If you remember what it said, that settles it in one line — otherwise Settings → Actions → General for that repo is the page that decides it.

Worth saying: approval only cost ~21 hours of *discovery latency* here. The build was going to be red either way.

input.title: A removed engine/pack export breaks members' local packs, and nothing gates it
input.body:
#1750 (`db9981f`) removed the pack-badge-row mechanism from `engine/converge-wiring.mjs`, dropping the exports `BADGE_ROW_START`, `BADGE_ROW_END`, `README`, `RULES_INDEX_MERGE_ATTR`, `SKILLS_INDEX_MERGE_ATTR`, `MOUNT_VENDORED_ATTR`, `badgeRowEntries`, `renderBadgeRow` and `convergeBadgeRow`. The three `ensure*` functions kept re-export shims; these nine did not.

Shepherd's own world rule imports three of them:

```
.claudinite/local/packs/shepherd/worldRules/pack-badge-row.mjs:2
  import { BADGE_ROW_START, BADGE_ROW_END, README } from '.../shared/engine/converge-wiring.mjs';
```

The 2026-09-06 converge delivered the new engine, the module failed to load, `check_the_world` reported it blocking under `config`, the converged tree failed its self-test, and missingbulb/Shepherd#477 is parked `needs-human`.

## Why neither gate saw it

Member local-pack code that imports engine surfaces is a real, corpus-encouraged contract that nothing treats as one.

- **The live canary.** `ClaudiniteCanary`'s local pack imports nothing out of `.claudinite/shared/` — `realism-artifacts.mjs:12` states it as a design property. A rehearsal converges it green whatever the engine's export surface does.
- **The fixture rehearsal.** No fixture local pack in `vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` imports an engine module either.
- **`consumer-safe-change`.** Narrowed to three surfaces — `pack-schema.mjs`, a rule's `severity`, the two workflow stubs. An engine module's exported symbols are not among them, so #1750 merged correctly per the check as written.

The existing prose rule names the shape one rung down — *"Renaming or deleting an `engine/` module a `packs/` file imports — leave a shim"* — but stops at modules, and addresses canon packs rather than members' local packs.

## The change

Widen `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/workRules/consumer-safe-change.mjs` with a fourth surface: an exported symbol present in a `.mjs` file's base and absent from its head, under `engine/**` or `packs/**`. Discharged by the existing pair (a migration record, a rehearsal fixture) or by the cheapest and most common answer — a re-export shim, which needs no new mechanism because a name still exported is not a removal.

Measured firing rate over the 60 most recent first-parent commits on `main`: 4 commits (1 engine, 3 packs), with #1750 a fifth just outside the window. `packs/**` is included because the surface is structurally identical — Shepherd's `fleet-issues-snapshot/worker.mjs` imports four modules out of `shared/packs/`.

Also sweeps `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/RULES.md:23`, which still instructs every session in every member to run `converge-wiring.mjs <owner/repo> --badges` — a flag the same change deleted.

Shepherd's side is missingbulb/Shepherd#478.

input.title: pack-badge-row world rule imports engine exports that no longer exist — the converge is red
input.body:
`.claudinite/local/packs/shepherd/worldRules/pack-badge-row.mjs:2` imports `BADGE_ROW_START`, `BADGE_ROW_END` and `README` from `.claudinite/shared/engine/converge-wiring.mjs`. The canon removed all three in missingbulb/Claudinite#1750, so the module fails to load, `check_the_world` reports it blocking under `config`, and #477 is parked `needs-human` with a failed self-test.

The rule guards a mechanism that no longer exists: the canon no longer converges a pack-badge row into a member's README, adoption no longer seeds one, and `converge-wiring.mjs --badges` — the command the rule's own `fix` text names — is gone. A row already in the README stays there and is removable by hand.

So the rule goes, rather than being repointed at anything.

#1750 (`db9981f`) removed the pack-badge-row mechanism from `engine/converge-wiring.mjs`, dropping the exports `BADGE_ROW_START`, `BADGE_ROW_END`, `README`, `RULES_INDEX_MERGE_ATTR`, `SKILLS_INDEX_MERGE_ATTR`, `MOUNT_VENDORED_ATTR`, `badgeRowEntries`, `renderBadgeRow` and `convergeBadgeRow`. The three `ensure*` functions kept re-export shims; these nine did not.

Shepherd's own world rule imports three of them:

```
.claudinite/local/packs/shepherd/worldRules/pack-badge-row.mjs:2
  import { BADGE_ROW_START, BADGE_ROW_END, README } from '.../shared/engine/converge-wiring.mjs';
```

The 2026-09-06 converge delivered the new engine, the module failed to load, `check_the_world` reported it blocking under `config`, the converged tree failed its self-test, and missingbulb/Shepherd#477 is parked `needs-human`.

## Why neither gate saw it

Member local-pack code that imports engine surfaces is a real, corpus-encouraged contract that nothing treats as one.

- **The live canary.** `ClaudiniteCanary`'s local pack imports nothing out of `.claudinite/shared/` — `realism-artifacts.mjs:12` states it as a design property. A rehearsal converges it green whatever the engine's export surface does.
- **The fixture rehearsal.** No fixture local pack in `vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` imports an engine module either.
- **`consumer-safe-change`.** Narrowed to three surfaces — `pack-schema.mjs`, a rule's `severity`, the two workflow stubs. An engine module's exported symbols are not among them, so #1750 merged correctly per the check as written.

The existing prose rule names the shape one rung down — *"Renaming or deleting an `engine/` module a `packs/` file imports — leave a shim"* — but stops at modules, and addresses canon packs rather than members' local packs.

## The change

Widen `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/workRules/consumer-safe-change.mjs` with a fourth surface: an exported symbol present in a `.mjs` file's base and absent from its head, under `engine/**` or `packs/**`. Discharged by the existing pair (a migration record, a rehearsal fixture) or by the cheapest and most common answer — a re-export shim, which needs no new mechanism because a name still exported is not a removal.

Measured firing rate over the 60 most recent first-parent commits on `main`: 4 commits (1 engine, 3 packs), with #1750 a fifth just outside the window. `packs/**` is included because the surface is structurally identical — Shepherd's `fleet-issues-snapshot/worker.mjs` imports four modules out of `shared/packs/`.

Also sweeps `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/RULES.md:23`, which still instructs every session in every member to run `converge-wiring.mjs <owner/repo> --badges` — a flag the same change deleted.

Shepherd's side is missingbulb/Shepherd#481.

1	# core
2	
3	Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a
4	pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to.
5	
6	**Mandatory.** `basics` `requires` this pack, so the closure vendors its content and materializes its
7	declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it
8	into members that already exist. Removing the entry is not an opt-out — it is drift, and `claudinite-lifecycle-declared`
9	reports it.
10	
11	## Rules (`RULES.md`)
12	
13	| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
14	|---|---|---|---|
15	| Reading a rule that arrived from Claudinite | high | correctness | prose: 43 words + checks (`shared-tree-edit-guard`, `shared-tree-immutable`, `claudinite-isolation`) |
16	| Finding a mounted skill's real path | medium | complexity | prose: 81 words |
17	| Wanting a pack's rules to apply here | high | correctness | prose: 47 words + check (`claudinite-lifecycle-declared`) |
18	| Renaming or removing a pack's declaration on a repo whose README still carries a legacy pack-badge row | medium | correctness | prose: 59 words |
19	| Adding a pack | medium | complexity | prose: 27 words |
20	| Setting a project up on Claudinite | medium | complexity | prose: 15 words |
21	| Deciding which pack owns a lesson | medium | complexity | prose: 59 words |
22	| Judging whether Claudinite is current here | medium | correctness | prose: 51 words |
23	| Answering "why did the mount not update" | medium | correctness | prose: 39 words |
24	| A referenced file absent from the mount | medium | correctness | prose: 56 words |
25	| An engine comment citing a design doc | low | complexity | prose: 53 words |
26	| A silent check run is clean | low | complexity | prose: 50 words |
27	| Pushing a change the world sweep scans | medium | complexity | prose: 49 words |
28	
29	## Checks
30	
31	Each of these asks the same kind of question: **is Claudinite working in this repo** — declared,
32	converged, gated, scheduled. A repo can fail any of them silently, which is why they are checks and
33	not prose: the session that has lost its rules is the session least able to notice.
34	
35	| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
36	|---|---|---|---|
37	| `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
38	| `rules-index-current` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
39	| `claudinite-isolation` | high | complexity | check: blocking |
40	| `shared-tree-edit-guard` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
41	| `shared-tree-immutable` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
42	| `conformance-workflow` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
43	| `conformance-work-scope` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
44	| `scheduler-workflow-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
45	| `legacy-shape-in-use` | medium | complexity | check: advisory |
46	| `skill-loaded-before-editing` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
47	| `skills-index-current` | medium | correctness | check: blocking |
48	
49	What goes wrong when one fires:
50	
51	- `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` — this pack's entry is gone from `.claudinite-settings.json`, so none of the rules above run and the session cannot tell.
52	- `rules-index-current` — the generated index is missing, stale or unimported: the repo's packs contribute no prose to any session.
53	- `claudinite-isolation` — the repo's own code reaches into `.claudinite/`, so the next canon refactor is a breaking migration for code the canon does not own (a declared `forbidReferences` barrier edge).
54	- `conformance-workflow` — nothing in CI runs the world sweep unfiltered on a pull request, so conformance is ungated and the maintenance PR never lands.
55	- `conformance-work-scope` — CI gates the tree but not the change, so every commit-scoped rule is enforced only where a session's Stop hook happens to run.
56	- `scheduler-workflow-shape` — the vendored scheduler's cron, concurrency or dispatch guard has drifted: staggering, double-run safety or manual runs break.
57	
58	The **task contract** and its checks are deliberately NOT here. Those ask whether a task is
59	*written* correctly, which is authoring; every check above asks whether Claudinite is *working* in
60	this repo. They live with the rest of the authoring surface.
61	
62	The scope cuts the other way too: a rule about how the **canon's own** content is maintained is not
63	this pack's, however much it looks like one. `catalog-completeness` — `packs/README.md` lists every
64	`packs/<name>/` — reads as Claudinite machinery and is not: it can only fire in the corpus repo, and
65	what it guards is a hand-maintained index, not a member's status. It stays with the other
66	doc-integrity rules.
67	
68	`skill-loaded-before-editing` is the Stop-time half of **path-scoped skills**: a skill names
69	the files it must be loaded for under `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` in its SKILL.md frontmatter
70	`metadata` (the harness's own `paths` is a limiter on when it offers a skill, so it cannot carry

72	loaded that skill, and this rule catches the edits the guard never saw (a `sed`, a heredoc) by
73	asking the diff the same question. Both read one resolver,
74	`engine/pack_loader/path-scoped-skills.mjs`. A load is a `Skill` tool call or a `Read` of the
75	skill's own SKILL.md. `skills-index-current` keeps the generated
76	`.claudinite/claudinite-skills.GENERATED.md` — every mounted skill with what loads it, the
77	scoped ones first — naming what the declared packs actually bundle.
78	
79	## Skills
80	
81	| Skill | For |
82	|---|---|
83	| [`adopt-claudinite`](skills/adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md) | setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time — mount, hooks, checks, skills — and re-baselining one to pick up updates |
84	| [`adopt-pack`](skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) | adding a pack to a repo that already runs Claudinite: declare, interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land |

104	loses its self-refresh, and nothing is left that could deliver it one. That is also why the task
105	arrived here a change later than the rest of the pack — it moved only once every non-dormant member's
106	declaration had been read back and confirmed to carry `core`.

# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking.
- **Reference the issue** — `Refs #n`, or `Fixes #n` / `Closes #n` where the commit finishes it;

- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.
- **Stage by name** — `git add <paths>` for the files this commit is about; `-a` sweeps in whatever
  else was in progress.

input.head: claude/build-break-investigation-lp4a8o
input.body:
Closes #1848

#1750 (`db9981f`) removed nine exports from `engine/converge-wiring.mjs`. Three of them — `BADGE_ROW_START`, `BADGE_ROW_END`, `README` — are imported by Shepherd's own world rule, so last night's converge delivered an engine its local pack could not load: `check_the_world` reported it blocking under `config`, the converged tree failed its self-test, and missingbulb/Shepherd#477 parked `needs-human`.

## Why nothing caught it

Member local-pack code importing the mount is a real, corpus-encouraged contract that nothing treated as one.

- **The live canary** — `ClaudiniteCanary`'s local pack imports nothing out of `.claudinite/shared/`; `realism-artifacts.mjs:12` states it as a design property. A rehearsal converges it green whatever the export surface does.
- **The fixture rehearsal** — no fixture local pack in `vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` imports an engine module either.
- **`consumer-safe-change`** — three surfaces, and an exported symbol was not one, so #1750 merged correctly per the check as written.

## The gate

A fourth surface: a name present in a `.mjs` file's base and absent from its head, under `engine/**` or `packs/**`, outside tests, `engine-tests/`, the canon's own local packs and dated migration records. A **re-export shim discharges it with no new mechanism** — a name still exported is not a removal, which is the answer #1750 already gave three of its nine names. The migration record and the rehearsal fixture stay available for a name that genuinely must go.

Deleting a module outright is covered: an unreadable head is every name it exported going away, which is the case a diff-line rule structurally cannot see.

## Evidence

- **See it fail:** six tests red against the unmodified rule, green after.
- **See it catch the real thing:** replaying `db9981f`'s own diff through `contractChanges` fires on `engine/converge-wiring.mjs` and names all nine removed exports.
- **Firing rate, measured before widening the scope:** over the 60 most recent first-parent commits on `main`, 4 would have fired (1 engine, 3 packs) — with #1750 a fifth just outside the window. `packs/**` is in because the surface is structurally identical: Shepherd's `fleet-issues-snapshot/worker.mjs` reaches four modules under `shared/packs/`.
- Whole suite green (3357 tests); `check_the_world` and `check_the_work` both 0 blocking.

## The second commit

`packs/claudinite-lifecycle/RULES.md` still told every session in every member to run `converge-wiring.mjs <owner/repo> --badges` — a flag the same PR deleted. The rule now names what survives: a README carrying a legacy row goes red on `reference-integrity` when a declared pack's `badge.svg` leaves the mount, and the badge has to be removed by hand.

`rules-append-only` reports that retirement as an advisory. It is deliberate, which is what its `fix` text asks be said here.

## Folders touched

| folder | what changed |
|---|---|
| `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/workRules/` | `consumer-safe-change.mjs` grows the removed-export surface: `exportedNames`, `removedExports`, and one entry per file in `contractChanges` |
| `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/` | `RULES.md` retires the `--badges` rule and restates the hazard that outlives it |

Shepherd's side, which unblocks its converge: missingbulb/Shepherd#481.

input.body:
Closes #481

`.claudinite/local/packs/shepherd/worldRules/pack-badge-row.mjs` imports `BADGE_ROW_START`, `BADGE_ROW_END` and `README` from `.claudinite/shared/engine/converge-wiring.mjs`. missingbulb/Claudinite#1750 removed all three, so once that engine reaches this mount the module throws at load, the pack fails to load, and `check_the_world` reports it blocking under `config`. That is why #477's converged tree failed its self-test and parked `needs-human`.

There is nothing to repoint the rule at. The canon no longer converges a pack-badge row into a member's README, adoption no longer seeds one, and `converge-wiring.mjs --badges` — the command the rule's own `fix` text names — is gone.

The second commit removes the `tidy-repo` badge from the README row. missingbulb/Claudinite#1839 absorbed that pack into `basics`, and the `2026-09-06-tidy-repo-absorbed` record renames this repo's declared entry on the next converge; the mount stops holding `packs/tidy-repo/` at the same moment, so the badge is about to point at a file that is not there and `reference-integrity` reports that as blocking — the same break #463 fixed for the `barriers` badge. Nothing re-derives the row any more, so it is a hand edit or nothing, and `basics` is already in the row.

`check_the_world` is 0 blocking with both changes applied.

## Folders touched

| folder | what changed |
|---|---|
| `.claudinite/local/packs/shepherd/worldRules/` | `pack-badge-row.mjs` deleted — the directory is now empty |

The canon-side gate that would have caught the export removal before it shipped is missingbulb/Claudinite#1850.

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with
  paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it, so a green run
  isn't coverage of it.

- **Scanning for a forbidden token** — strip comments first so it matches code, not prose —
  string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);
  if the scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.
  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either.

- **Proving the check silent** — run it against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.
